c49b7427ae3d9b49: The success of South Korean popular music or K-pop continues to power the Hallyu Wave, a term that describes the global obsession with the country’s pop culture production. But before K-pop came the spread of K-drama, TV series from the country, starting in the late 1990s. By 2024 the melodrama Queen of Tears ranked as the most watched Korean series on Netflix, becoming the 14th most watched show of all time on the streaming service. It followed on the success of many other hits like Crash Landing on You and Marry My Husband. K-drama has led to the development of another trend: Africa repeatedly appears as a homogeneous place full of savage danger or childish immaturity, and in need of a Korean saviour. As a scholar of film and media, with a specific interest in global Black art and film practices, I recently studied how and why Africa became this trope in K-drama. This is particularly true in rags-to-riches romance stories and melodramas. I traced Africa’s presence in three K-dramas – Shooting Stars (2022), Marry My Husband (2024) and Queen of Tears (2024). In them, Africa appears in three different negative ways: in need of charity a place of rebellion and savagery a place of punishment for a “troubled” child. My intention wasn’t to say why these portrayals are bad, but rather to understand what they reveal about South Korea. How they function as a scale for measuring and emphasising South Korea’s own development. No longer the poor post-war country of the late 1950s, South Korea can now position itself among leading world powers. It has grown in the global economic and cultural landscapes. Yet, as I argue in my study, what allows countries like this to define their developmental status is their ability to distinguish themselves from Africa. I propose that Africa’s presence in K-dramas is as a place maker, or specifically image-maker. Africa’s “savage” presence serves as a way of distinguishing the emerging soft power of South Korea, where what benefits the country’s global image is the ability to provide aid to Africa. A place to do good In his book On the Postcolony, Cameroonian philosopher Achille Mbembe describes Africa as Europe’s “signifier”. This means that the way Europe comes to know and define itself is only possible through how it defines itself against Africa. But my study contributes to showing that this is not just the case in the west. The ever-growing presence of eastern soft powers such as China and South Korea means that longstanding stereotypes of Africa have found new sites of replenishment. There are some major threads that connected Africa’s presence in the K-dramas I studied. One is its portrayal as a place where non-Africans could go to build character by participating in volunteer work as part of an NGO. In Marry my Husband, for example, the show’s antagonist Oh Yu-ra loses her job in the family business and is sent to “join a volunteer foundation in Africa to build character”. In Shooting Stars, this idea of Africa as the epicentre of charity is even more apparent. The show’s opening sequence features the main character digging wells in Africa. He’s accompanied by smiling village children and a sound that one viewer described as “Lion King music”. In both shows, South Korea is personified through the characters sent to Africa. While Yu-ra is sent as punishment, the character in Shooting Stars is an actor whose volunteer trip aids in his public image in South Korea. Africa becomes what builds the image and character of others, but only by being relegated to a cliché. Yu-ra’s punishment shows how Africa becomes the K-drama’s vessel to hold the unwanted or defamed of other nations. It collects what disrupts the happiness of romance and, by extension, of nation-making, in South Korea. This figuration of the continent reappears in Queen of Tears. A lawless continent Queen of Tears does not follow the Asian-saviour-in-Africa trope. Instead, it presents Africa as a place for youthful inhibitions, with no sense of order or rule of law. The ideal place for the kinds of behaviours that might be illegal in the more “civilized” South Korean society that the character exists in. In Africa’s brief cameo in the show’s third episode, the younger brother of the show’s protagonist, Soo-Cheol, reminisces on his rebellious days: I’m reminded of when I went to Africa. My twenties were filled with wildness and barbarism. When chided that he stayed in his hotel for most of the trip, Soo-Cheol comments, “I had enough of the wildness just looking out of the window.” Here, Africa is understood in proximity to danger and savagery. Is it that there are no crime, criminals, or places and people in need of saving in South Korea? The obvious answer is no, but as my study finds, when viewed through these shows, the answer reads more like, “Compared to Africa, yes.” Where will Africa go next? This treatment of Africa began long before the shows in my study. Africa’s character-building qualities appear, for example, in the 2018 film Burning. The film’s female protagonist goes on a “soul-searching” quest to find life’s greater meaning. In unscripted variety shows, African immigrants living in South Korea, like Sam Okyere or Jonathan Yiombi, often feature as hosts or guests, but not without their share of racist backlash. Okyere, for example, was subject to racist comments after criticising a video of South Korean students recreating a popular video from his home country, Ghana. The same happened to Yiombi after South Korea was eliminated from the football World Cup because the DRC, his country of birth, defeated Uzbekistan, indirectly causing South Korea to be eliminated. For better or worse, Africa’s metaphorical and literal presence has come to occupy South Korea’s cultural and aesthetic imagination. Despite Africa also being a continent full of modern urban life, cultural riches and innovation, the clichés remain. Read more: Streaming giants have helped bring Korean dramas to the world – but much is lost in translation This presence is only possible through the expected and invented image of the savage, helpless and primitive, who is in need, even after independence, of more civilising. And not only from western colonial powers, but also from the growing economies of the east. A symbol of lack K-dramas are increasingly popular in Africa, yet when constantly viewed this way, Hallyu’s success in Africa comes with a heavy representational price. Despite their engagement with K-drama, African audiences can only ever seem to see themselves represented through a colonial gaze that benefits South Korea’s pursuit of global power. Africa then, while continuing to build South Korea’s cultural capital, can only ever exist as a symbol of lack. b5b93da943d07b75: daily_creativity/Shutterstock After two decades of decline, the number of executions in the United States began rising sharply again in 2025. Last year, 47 people were put to death – the highest number in more than 15 years. So far in 2026, another 31 people have been executed. The resurgence comes amid renewed controversy over capital punishment, following the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee and a proposal to livestream a military execution, which President Donald Trump subsequently walked back. But according to Carolyn Strange, emeritus professor of history at the Australian National University, these controversies have striking precedents in American history. Pike is not the first person to survive an execution attempt. In 1946, Willie Francis survived the electric chair in Louisiana. After an unsuccessful legal challenge, the state executed him in 1947. Strange says the history of capital punishment in the US is marked by repeated attempts to make executions more humane – or at least appear that way. From the electric chair to lethal injections, new methods were introduced with the promise of making death quicker and more efficient. Lethal injection, for example, has the appearance of an ordinary medical procedure. “It seems normal, it seems clean, it seems clinical, civilised,” Strange says. Yet Pike’s case raises questions about whether the method has lived up to that promise. Strange also argues it’s misleading to talk about a single American approach to the death penalty. It’s really better to talk about the death penalty in the disunited states. While some states abolished capital punishment more than a century ago, others continue to embrace it. Florida, under governor Ron DeSantis, has been responsible for a substantial share of the recent rise in executions. In 2025, Florida carried out 19 executions – 40% of the year’s total. And while support in the US for the death penalty has declined over recent decades, the issue remains deeply divisive. For Strange, the history of capital punishment reveals something fundamental about American politics: The most important thing is that capital punishment and the death penalty is about politics, not justice. 8505edd61e75c03b: Students protest in Place de la Bastille, Paris, in October 2026. davidezambon/ShutterstockYoung people are facing a future that feels increasingly uncertain. Although every generation experiences turbulence while navigating adolescence, the pressures experienced by Gen Z – those born between 1997 and 2012 – are different and seem more pervasive. From climate change and mental health concerns to academic pressure, housing costs, job and economic insecurity, today’s young people are navigating a complex set of expectations. Understanding their frustrations, including those expressed through protests across Europe, requires looking beyond individual experiences to the social conditions shaping their lives. Adolescence has long been seen as a period of “storm and stress”. This reflecting a belief that is a universal and inevitable period of emotional turmoil, behavioural conflict and identity crisis. However, this has been increasingly challenged. Rather than being defined solely by difficulty and disruption, adolescence is increasingly viewed as a period of possibility, opportunity and growth. Yet realising that potential depends heavily on the social environments in which young people grow up. A growing body of evidence highlights adolescence as a critical developmental period with profound implications for future health and wellbeing. There is also increasing recognition that adolescence extends well beyond the teenage years and well into the twenties. Growing up under pressure Young people nowadays grow up under intense and often overlapping pressure, and today this is to a higher extent than generations before. Evidence from the World Health Organization’s Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study suggests that school-related pressure increased between 2002 and 2022 across many countries. In 2022, among 15-year-old girls, almost two-thirds reported feeling pressured by schoolwork, compared with less than half of boys. The same research documented declines in perceived family and peer support. In other words, young people appear to be facing increasing demands while some of the social resources that help them cope with those demands are weakening. Young people are feeling educational pressure. Fotokut/Shutterstock Parental expectations and criticism have also intensified in many contexts. Success is increasingly framed as an individual responsibility, while educational pathways have become more competitive. At the same time, social media can amplify processes of social comparison, putting young people’s achievements, appearance and lifestyles under constant public scrutiny. For many, there is little respite from the pressure to perform. Economic concerns add another level of pressure. Rising living costs, high tertiary education expanses and uncertainty about future employment rank among young people’s greatest worries. Across the EU, 40% are highly concerned by rising prices and the cost of living. In 2026, national surveys show that around 70% of Irish adolescents consider emigration for better life conditions. Over 20% of Dutch secondary school students are concerned whether they will ever be able to afford a home. A warming planet and an uncertain future Today’s young people are growing up amid an increasingly visible climate crisis. They hear repeated warnings about the short- and long-term consequences of climate change. Their generation will be disproportionally affected, and they know it. For some, this contributes to feelings of anxiety, worry, sadness, anger and helplessness about environmental degradation and the future. Concerns like this about a genuine global threat can be a rational and entirely understandable response. What can make these concerns particularly difficult is the perception that the decisions affecting young people’s future are often made without their meaningful involvement or consideration of their needs. This cycle of intergenerational injustice needs to be acknowledged and addressed. When people feel they have little influence on issues that will meaningfully shape their lives, this can lead to frustration. Evidence from many countries suggest that Gen Z are experiencing poorer mental health than previous generations. Although patterns vary across cultures and contexts, large scale studies point to increasing levels of emotional distress and psychological difficulties among young people. Public discussions often focus on explanations at an individual level: excessive screen time, reduced resilience and difficulties coping with everyday challenges. While these factors may play a role, they do not account for the whole story. Mental health is shaped by the interaction between individual experiences and wider social, economic and cultural environments in which people live. As such, the current rise in mental health difficulties should not be understood as a solely individual problem. Rather, it reflects a response to broader societal pressures that young people face as they move towards adulthood. Despite these challenges, it would be wrong to portray Gen Z as a generation defined only by anxiety or pessimism. Protests concerning housing, education, climate policy and economic inequality can express frustration, but they also demonstrate agency and a desire to influence decisions about the future. A 2025 survey of 6,703 young people across Europe found that 80% of young respondents in Germany considered EU membership a good thing, up from 65% in 2024. In France, the figure rose from 53% to 60%. The study also highlighted the importance young people attach to making the cost of living affordable. These findings challenge the assumption that today’s young generation is simply disengaged from society. Young people are not passive recipients of social pressures. They organise, question existing arrangements and seek alternatives. The difficulties facing Gen Z are not entirely new. What makes their experience distinctive is the combination of pressures and the uncertainty surrounding the transition to adulthood. Rather than asking whether today’s young people have it harder than previous generations, we should ask more productive questions: what kind of society are we asking them to navigate? And what can be done to make it healthier, fairer and more hopeful? <!--kg-card-end: html--> For much of the last month, many of the cybersecurity experts I talk to and follow have been posting like they are very scared. Many have been warning of an AI-powered “Black Swan” event, have been alarmed by the number of vulnerabilities suddenly discovered, and of the apparent power of AI agents and large language models more broadly to find and exploit previously unknown bugs.

The rhetoric has ranged from worried-but-measured (things are about to get weird), to run-of-the-mill advice like update your software and make sure you have two-factor authentication on, to vagueposting about AI-powered attacks, to things like ‘the internet was nice while it lasted,’ to outright prepper-level terror.

To give you a sense of what I’m seeing, Matthew Green, a Johns Hopkins professor and one of the most respected cryptographers in the world, posted “we’re in the part of the movie where you need to throw whatever you can in the path of the zombies and hope it slows them down,” and “so many people discovering that the whole Internet is dry tinder and the only thing keeping it from burning is the fact that teenagers haven’t found the matches yet,” Green is alluding to the fact that hackers and researchers driving AI tools and agents are getting better at finding and exploiting all sorts of bugs in important systems. I’ve also seen numerous AI employees, as mentioned, go full prepper, suggesting people pull money out of their bank accounts, disconnect from the internet, purchase shelf-stable food, hoard water, put money in gold and cash, and purchase hand-crank emergency radios.

And all those posts came before people using AI-powered tools found vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers much of the internet. In the last few days, major vulnerabilities or issues have been found in eMudhra (an Indian entity that provides website security certificates), Node.js (an alternative to PHP), Gitlab (a software development platform), Plex (media server software), Railway (a cloud provider), OpenCode (a coding agent platform), and several other companies and services, though, rightfully, none of these has gotten as much attention as the vulnerabilities in PHP, called PHP2Shell, which researchers from Wiz, Calif, and OpenAI discovered using AI.

Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, a service that has wide insight into the general health of the internet, posted, “In the 10 hours before [PHP2Shell] was publicly announced, across the Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.”

So much is happening, and so quickly, that it has been difficult for me — someone who has been reporting and editing stories on security and hacking for a decade — to fully understand what’s going on, to have a sense of what could happen next, or predict where this is going. And I think that that is largely where we are at the moment, as I am writing this.

But it has become clear that AI, broadly defined, has fundamentally changed both offensive hacking and defensive cybersecurity. This is not because AI has become sentient or because human beings have lost control of it or because of “swarms” of “rogue agents,” but because AI is proving something that we have always known: much of the software that runs the internet, our devices, our accounts, and our lives is vulnerable, or out of date, or has security flaws that human beings never noticed, or was installed by someone at a company who left the company six years ago and has been replaced four times and no one knows how to find them now or how to update it. This doesn’t mean that all of the vulnerabilities that have been found with the help of AI have been obvious or trivial; skilled hackers and researchers, driving AI tools, seem to be better than humans alone at finding vulnerabilities. But, critically, AI and large language models have made it extremely easy to essentially brute force the internet; if every piece of software is a door, AI makes it exceptionally easy to turn turn the knobs of every door to see if it’s unlocked, even on buildings that human beings had never really bothered to try to open. What we are learning at an alarmingly fast pace is that not only are some of the locks easy to pick, in some cases the door is wide open or there’s a giant hole in the wall. The recent spate of people using AI to hack their internet of things devices to run new software shows that, in some cases, it takes essentially no expertise to actually use AI to hack something.

Meanwhile, we've seen the rise of "abliterated" AI models that are designed to not say no and open weights models that can be used for pentesting and potentially offensive hacks without the guardrails that exist in many off-the-shelf commercial models.

In a blog post explaining the PHP vulnerability discovery, OpenAI said the findings highlight “how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.” OpenAI basically argues that it did all of this research ethically, and that its discovery opened a “Defender’s Window” that allowed governments and critical infrastructure to prepare for the disclosure of the bug. ‘Researcher finds bug, ethically discloses it to company, company fixes it’ is the preferred course of action in cybersecurity, but AI is shortening the window for all of this, is leading more people to do more research more easily, and is making both bug finding and bug fixing much faster. Whether those fixes are actually deployed by individual companies any faster is another, much more complicated question. The answer in many cases is, probably, no.

AI is also making all of this much more unpredictable. The security company Chainguard was criticized for breaking the embargo on the PHP vulnerability disclosure because it posted fixes for the vulnerabilities several hours before it was officially disclosed. Critics, including the PHP Foundation, said this could have let attackers figure out how to exploit the issues before website owners had a chance to protect their systems. In a LinkedIn post, Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc said that his company independently found the same bugs by typing “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP” into a frontier AI model. Amazon, meanwhile, said that it saw exploit attempts before the official disclosure. These facts raise questions about whether the bug was exceptionally easy to find, whether the AI models that originally found the vulnerabilities incorporated that information into the model somehow therefore making it easier for someone else to find, or whether there was a leak along the way from someone connected to the disclosure process. Any option is concerning.

After the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were discovered, some infosec experts started calling this “Black October,” and highlighted the fact that the National Security Agency, the Prime Minister of Japan, and various governments around the world told people to patch their websites and services immediately, and to take down services that couldn’t be patched. 4chan, several Wikimedia services, and Archive.org were all temporarily taken offline so that they could be updated.

As The Atlantic has already suggested, one of the biggest impacts of PHP2Shell could be the fact that many historic websites can’t or won’t be updated, may be proactively pulled offline, might eventually be hacked, and might never come back. The link rot could be horrendous, and a lot of history could be lost.

For such a high-profile incident, most of the actual impacts thus far have been related to the proactive patching or removal of potentially insecure websites, and we have not seen immediate, widespread exploitation of the bug. Various low-effort, LLM-developed exploits have been dropped online; many of them will not work. A blog post called “There isn’t an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability,” written by Elias Taylor, quickly went viral and was dissected on Hacker News, especially by people pointing out that the website eliastaylor.com had been recently registered and that it wasn’t clear who Elias Taylor was. 404 Media reached Taylor by Signal; he said “I am real and on a delayed train.”

“Lots of people are being tricked by AI into thinking they have an exploit when they don't, because they can't read or understand what the LLM gave them,” Taylor told 404 Media. “It doesn't appear to be anywhere near as exploitable as the other ‘stop the world’ vulnerabilities i.e log4j, heartbleed. But patch your servers, it’s still a vulnerability. Please do not paraphrase me as saying ‘there is no vulnerability’ for any reason. There is, and people should patch.”

Dan Guido, the CEO of Trail of Bits, a well-respected cybersecurity company that partners with OpenAI on the Patch the Planet initiative, posted that his company had created “a working exploit,” and that “Will Tan built it in 1 day with Codex, drawing on ~10 years of system security and vulnerability research. AI accelerates exploit development. Knowing how to turn a bug into a shell still takes expertise. AI makes that expertise more productive.”

It should also be noted that Taylor’s other blog post is called “Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces,” which includes the lines “software engineers have spent the past 40 years writing vulnerable, dogshit software. LLMs are easily above the bar needed to break into said software.”

It remains unclear, at the moment, what the ultimate impact of all of this is going to be, or where we’ll be in one hour, one week, one year, or 10 years. But AI is changing how cybersecurity and hacking works. It is making finding and exploiting bugs faster and easier. We’re about to find out how insecure the internet really is.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> The UN met this week to discuss, among other things, the threat of autonomous weapons.

“The technology is developing at a pace that is very concerning,” Laurent Gisel, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) legal warfare team, told 404 Media. Gisel was in NYC this week to address the UN about all the things that are driving conflict across the planet. His prepared remarks include a statement on the illegal arms trade, nuclear weapons, mines, and – of course – AI.

Autonomous weapons have been a hot topic at the UN this year. In September, the UN attempted to pass a treaty that would govern the use of killer AI weapons. Diplomats from Russia and the US stripped it of its power.

But the UN has pressed forward. On Tuesday, the international governing body announced a new initiative that would grapple with the issue. But, as Gisel said: “multilateral processes take quite some time” and “we already see the effects on the battlefield.”
AI is already picking targets and killing people. Gisel said the technology is “amplifying the destruction, amplifying the violation of the law, amplifying the humanitarian harm caused by conflicts.”

Israel used an AI powered by Microsoft to pick targets in Gaza. In Ukraine, AI-powered Russian drones are deciding which humans to kill. The United States military is pitching itself as an “AI-first” fighting force. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth recently announced Project Meridian, an initiative to guide the AI-powered autonomous weapons of the future. Three of Meridian's leads are Elon Musk, defense contractor Palmer Luckey, and Newt Gingrich.

For Gisel, one of the biggest dangers of AI is how fast it is. A core selling point for the tech is that it can help commanders make decisions faster. But that also accelerates the pace of mistakes. “Targets are created at higher speed and higher frequency, and are actually then prosecuted quicker, and with that give us great concerns in terms of the level of human control that is retained,” he said. “The human is supposed to remain in the loop.”

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The human does not always remain in the loop. The Israel Defense Forces told journalists it did not thoroughly vet the kill lists generated by Lavender, the AI system it used to pick targets in Gaza. “It's known in the [civilian world] [...] that humans tend to trust the systems,” Gisel said. “That it's more the case when the humans are tired, when the humans are under stress, when the humans have to deliver quickly, and that's of course exactly the situation in which soldiers are in. So all of that gives us a lot of concerns in terms of retaining control on the use of force in armed conflict.”

AI boosters often pitch AI as an “easy button,” a way for people to brute force a complicated task and get it over with. But the consequences are much different when someone in Silicon Valley is parsing spreadsheets or reverse engineering code than when they’re prosecuting a war in the Middle East.

“That's something that the developers of those systems don't necessarily realize either, because some of those systems are developed by technological companies very far away from the battlefield, and they are not naturally all developed for battlefield use,” Gisel said.

International humanitarian law is an ever-evolving legal negotiation between world powers meant to limit the devastating effects of war. It’s imperfect and countries with vast armies like the US and Russia often do not abide by it. The ICRC, which Gisel represents, exists explicitly to shape these rules and laws. Some of the laws are old, far older than AI, but according to Gisel humanitarian law applies to “all weapons, means, and methods of warfare. Those of yesterday, those of today, and those of tomorrow.”

Beyond the opportunity to code humanitarian law into AI, Gisel said there should be new rules and regulations for the new technology. “Not to prohibit them all, but to prohibit specific categories of autonomous weapon systems and put specific restrictions on others,” he said.
"...Once the genie is out of the bottle, it's very, very much difficult to put it back in the bottle"

But he does have redlines. The first is any AI support system that removes a human being from the kill chain. “That requires specific limits and guardrails and restrictions from our perspective,” he said.

“The other type of autonomous weapon system that we recommend prohibiting is those that would target human beings directly, where the target profile is the human being, as opposed to a tank, weapon systems, or another typical military objective, and the reason why is based on ethical concerns, humanitarian concerns, and a moral line,” he added.

Autonomous weapons have existed for a long time. Some US warships have gatling guns that track and destroy incoming targets automatically. The difference is that those weapons track ships and missiles, not human beings.

According to Gisel, one problem with autonomous weapons that target humans or AI support systems that pick targets is that they’re unpredictable. He said banning unpredictable weapons should be a non-brainer. “Military discipline is about your forces [...] delivering the commander's intent,” he said. “If you have a weapon that is unpredictable in its effect, how can you deliver the commander's intent?”
Data Centers Are War Targets Now
"Why have we gotten to the point where we have permitted militaries of various states to use civilian commercial data centers for their military purposes?"

But it’s been a sticking point in negotiations. “We would have thought, military considerations, would align. But actually, that has also faced quite some pushback. Strangely enough,” he said. He spoke about the negotiations in August and September from earlier in the year. “There were references in the last proposal by the chair of the group on precisely all those questions: that the autonomous weapon systems need to be reliable, explainable, understandable, and predictable. And all of that was taken out by some states.”

Gisel also opposes AI in nuclear command and control. In 1983, the Soviet Union’s early warning systems reported that the US had launched a nuclear weapon at the country. Soviet lieutenant colonel Stanislav Petrov decided the computer had made a mistake and decided not to report the attacks up the chain. He was right.

“States will continue to use satellite systems and therefore algorithms that go with those satellites,” he said. “But it's so important to ensure that it remains entirely under human control and a really meaningful human control.”

While the UN deliberates and the ICRC wrangles with how to regulate all this, the wars continue and military forces continue to embrace AI. “That's why it's urgent to have decisions being made by the international community on what to prohibit and what to restrict [...] once the genie is out of the bottle, it's very, very much difficult to put it back in the bottle,” he said.
Gisel said the world needs to act now. “Otherwise, it's the technology that will decide what is acceptable, and that's not the world we want to live in, right?”
63242927e56562bc: When I first saw Katsushika Hokusai’s Clear Day with a Southern Breeze (also known as Red Fuji, 1830-1833), I was struck by its lustrous red resonating against the receding blue of the sky. Clouds align gently in an almost humorous formation. Near the peak of the mountain, are creases of snow. At its foot we are drawn to a multitude of tiny trees amassed in chorus. Easy to overlook, they change the picture. The great mountain becomes itself in relation to everything that surrounds it. Dulwich Picture Gallery is showing all of Hokusai’s 36 Views of Mount Fuji, including ten added after the series became popular. Hokusai made them in his seventies in the early 1830s as cheap prints for ordinary people in Edo (today’s Tokyo). It is the first, and perhaps only, time the complete series will be shown together in the UK. One image is instantly recognisable: The Great Wave (actually titled Under the Wave off Kanagawa). Seen alongside the others, it becomes one view among many – and a lesson in how quickly we settle on a single view of anything, including each other. Three versions of Mount Fuji hang together in the first room. In Red Fuji the mountain is almost pure form. A light blue variant, its ridge edged in heavy indigo, opens a way into the mountain. A third, with lightning like cracks in a pot, feels dark and unsettled. On the opposite wall hangs The Great Wave. Its foam reaches out like grasping, knuckled fingers, and flecks scatter across the dark water like stars in the night. Everything should be in motion, yet the print holds a stillness. Beneath the wave is Fuji again: a tiny triangle here where Red Fuji’s was expansive. It is the same mountain, but now framed by the sea. Elsewhere, people hurry over bridges, work in fields and travel along roads. Hills seem to wear patterned bandanas of farmland, while Prussian blue skies fade at a soft, feathered edge. Shapes mingle playfully: three haystacks echo the three small peaks of Fuji’s summit. Hokusai places us in between, looking down on people and up at the sky, but never from a position that reveals everything. In the third room, one print stopped me. In Mishima Pass in Kai Province, travellers link arms around an enormous tree. I saw an affectionate embrace, then learned they may be measuring its girth. How quickly I had decided what these strangers felt. As an art psychotherapist, I work with exactly this. We imagine what others might be thinking and feeling, drawing on our own experience – therapists call this mentalising, and doing it well means staying with curiosity rather than assuming we know. I have never been to Japan and cannot experience Fuji as Hokusai’s first viewers did. What reaches me is what colour, form and shape do, across that distance. Hokusai’s giant tree also recalls an experiment on awe in which people who had gazed up at towering eucalyptus trees for a minute picked up more of a researcher’s “accidentally” dropped pens than those who had looked at a building. A print may not make us kinder, but when we do feel part of a bigger picture, we may just become a bit less absorbed in ourselves, and perhaps more open to others. The curation is less subtle than the prints. Its dusky blue walls echo Hokusai’s colours, but I was left cold. I felt fixed as a viewer, each picture held apart when I wanted to see how they connect – although the soft lighting creates an atmosphere, a quietness that simply lets you be with them. At the end of the series, pilgrims climb into Fuji itself. Each looks much like the next, like frames of a stop-motion film. Near the summit they crowd into a shelter in the rock, a small window into something none could enter alone. We no longer look towards a distant mountain; we are drawn into it, among people making their own way upwards. I left thinking about The Great Wave very differently. I could see the little mountain beneath it, but also the trees, travellers and pilgrims. The Fuji I began with had amassed a sense of journey, unfolding across the series. Hokusai: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji from the Iuchi Collection is on at Dulwich Picture Gallery, London until January 17, 2027 Dominik Havsteen-Franklin does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

TRANSCRIPT:
At The Money: Dividend Growth Investing with David Bahnsen
Part 2 — Bloomberg Radio

David Bahnsen is founder, managing partner and chief investment officer of The Bahnsen Group, a national private wealth management firm. His new book is Profit from the Profit: The Past, Present, and Future of Dividend Growth Investing.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Dividends are one of the oldest and most highly regarded forms of equity investing. But in an era of mega-cap growth stocks, should you own dividend-paying equities? To help us unpack all of this and what it means for your portfolio, my extra special guest is David Bahnsen. He is the founder and chief investment officer of The Bahnsen Group and author of a brand-new book, Profit from the Profit: The Past, Present, and Future of Dividend Growth Investing. Welcome, David. Thank you so much for joining us.
DAVID BAHNSEN: Good to be with you, Barry.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So let’s start with first principles. Given the current environment with AI and semiconductors and tech, which tend not to pay dividends, why should investors care about dividends when really it’s all about total return these days?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, I don’t think it’s ever a matter of dividends versus total return. It’s a way in which people get to total return. And I think that you bring up a great point: the big tech moment caused some people to believe they don’t need dividends, they don’t need value, they don’t need valuation. We think that the way the dot-com tech moment ended is somewhat of a rebuttal to that thinking. It didn’t end very well.

We are in a moment in this AI period where some of the largest free-cash-flow-generating companies in history are now negative free cash flow because the capex is so high. We don’t want to make a call on how that’s going to play out. We would just simply suggest that there’s a different risk profile when companies are returning capital from free cash flow to shareholders — still profitable, still growing profits, healthy balance sheets. And by the way, there are some great dividend growers even within the AI world. Our ownership of Broadcom over a seven-year period is one of the most profitable investments we ever had.

You can’t really have the AI moment without data centers. Blackstone is one of the great dividend growers of the last decade. So it just takes the research to go find the right names that fit into the narrative.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So let’s stay with that point. What does it reveal about a company and its business when they’re willing to consistently pay a dividend, consistently increase that dividend? What does that tell us that sometimes earnings reports might not catch?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, dividends don’t lie. They’re cash. And it’s a line I’ve used many times over the last 25 years, Barry: there are plenty of people whose tax return shows an income that’s lower than what they really make. But there’s nobody whose tax return shows an income that’s higher than they really make. People don’t pay taxes on income they didn’t make. A dividend is real, and it reflects something real. In EBITDA you have a lot of opportunities for, let’s just say, not totally verifiable growth of a company. And so free cash flow is pure. A dividend from it reflects management’s confidence in the growth of the business. A slowing growth of the dividend maybe reflects management’s own view, but there’s nobody who should have a better view of things.
And you could trust their press releases if you want. You can trust the 10-Qs and what they say. But I really trust cash they put in my bank account.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So let’s distinguish between companies, especially mature businesses, that continue to grow their dividends versus those companies that seem to be running out of ways to manage their cash.

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, that’s a very important distinction, and it’s not just managing their cash, but it’s growing their business. Look, there’s no company that should never get to a point of cash flow productivity. When you are growing and you have infinite reinvestment opportunities where you’re getting a higher return on invested capital than the investor can get, you should be continuing to reinvest your own cash.

But eventually there is no infinity of what a company can do with that cash. So what do they end up doing when they don’t want to return it? They either just hold onto it and manage it in their own cash management vehicles — Apple’s been doing this forever. So do you want Apple holding on to hundreds of billions of cash in their own cash management vehicles? Or what do companies really end up doing most of the time? CEOs are notorious for M&A, and I would suggest that most M&A has served to be vanity projects and capital destructive. Now, not all — there are some that have been very synergistic. But when you look at the kind of return on equity that is generated from the great dividend growers over time, when they mature to a point that they can do it, their returns are unlike anything we’ve ever seen in history.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m glad you brought up Apple, which has become very well known for a massive stock buyback program over the past 10, 15 years. How do you compare the usage of free cash flow to either issue a dividend or to buy stock back? They’re both a return of capital to investors, but in a very different structure.

DAVID BAHNSEN: The problem, Barry, is that more often than not, they’re not a way to return capital to shareholders. How do you have record levels of share buybacks and yet more shares that exist now than did before all these share buybacks? The math is what it is. And so you have to look to net share issuance. And if they’re doing share buybacks, the net share issuance should be negative. But why has it grown leaps and bounds? Because for the most part — I’m not picking on Apple here or any particular company, but across the spectrum, and Silicon Valley’s notorious for this — share buybacks are executive compensation. They are not return of capital to shareholders.

Now, where companies are reducing their share count, that is a way to return capital to shareholders, and I’m all for it as a both/and. But my argument is that to the extent many investors are retirement oriented, they’re cash flow oriented, they need periodic income — you can’t eat a stock buyback. And so there is still something that is just tangible about receiving the cash of it. But the other issue is share buybacks go first whenever a company runs into trouble, and dividends tend to be last, because of that social contract that has been created by great dividend growers over long periods of time. So from the financial crisis of ’08 to the COVID moment, we saw this: share buybacks all but evaporated. For the great dividend growers — and I can speak to the portfolio we manage — we had zero dividend cuts through that horrible period. So it isn’t a hundred percent immune from the risk, but it’s far more immune from it than share buybacks.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m so glad you brought that up, because the question always comes up: when is a dividend sustainable? So what measures do you look at? Is it free cash flow or growth rate or earnings stability? Why not just buy the stocks with the highest dividend yield?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, the sustainability of the dividend is a very different question than why not buy the ones at the highest yield. Because the highest yield often could be a very imminent dividend cut — what I refer to as accidental high yielders. It’s just math, right? You have a 4% yield, a hundred-dollar stock price, you’re getting four bucks, and then the stock goes down to 50. You’re still getting four bucks, but now it’s 8%. Did you really get anything better? No. Did you lose 50% of your value? Yes. That’s not what we want. We want the yield going higher because the dividend’s going higher. And so there’s a big difference between a high yielder and a dividend grower.

Now, what do we look to? You mentioned three or four quantitative metrics. The answer is all of the above and then some. But where I just simply do not believe this can be done quantitatively, exclusively or passively, is in that qualitative element of when a company wants to pay the dividend, not when they’ve been dragged into doing it. So there is a cultural propensity to grow the dividend. Some C-suites do not like it, and we want to avoid those. Some where you have heavy founder ownership — I think of a company like Lamar Advertising or Enterprise Products Partners, which is still heavily owned by the family that started the company. They’re receiving just billions of dollars of dividends each year. They want to keep growing those dividends. So we like those stories where the alignment of management and shareholder is there.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So you mentioned the stock that got cut in half, and it appears the dividend yield has doubled when in reality it’s four bucks either way. That’s a classic yield trap, a classic dividend trap. What are the warning signs investors should be aware of when, hey, this looks like it’s high yield, but really it’s a dividend cut waiting to happen?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, one of the issues I believe has been a career saver or career maker for me, Barry — you of course were a prolific writer at the time of the financial crisis — I sold Citigroup stock at $51 a share when they announced they weren’t cutting their dividend in October of 2007, and it went to 97 cents. And so I don’t want to confuse everyone if they’re looking at charts now; reverse stock splits have confused everything. But I’m talking in 2007 numbers. This stock really did go down 99%, as you know.

So why did I sell the stock at $51 and then spend the next few years bragging to clients that we did? Because they said, “We’re not cutting the dividend, but we just borrowed $10.5 billion from the Saudi Arabians and Kuwaitis” at, I think it was, a 10% coupon on the debt. Borrowing from your credit card to pay your bills is not how a dividend gets sustained, as you and I know. Citi was a great example. So you have to look to the qualitative realities of the business. And when a company’s at $4 and they’ve been growing it for 20 years and they stop growing it, but they haven’t cut it yet — that’s a warning sign. When the rate of growth slows, that’s a warning sign. So we look to the free cash flow, the business model, the competition that’s come in, the investment thesis. It requires fundamental research. It is true.

The Procter & Gambles, the Exxon Mobils, the McDonald’s, the Johnson & Johnsons — they’ve managed to a payout ratio, a balance sheet, a cash flow that’s enabled them to continue growing through thick and thin. Other companies are too tight; they’re paying out 90% already and there’s no margin for error. So we have to take that a little more seriously. But this is why I believe it requires some active management. We’ve done it well over the years. A lot of people that really are invested in this have done well with it, but it isn’t foolproof. General Electric cut their dividend. AT&T cut their dividend. But there were clear warning signs those were coming for those paying attention.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I like the example of Citigroup, and you and I can swap war stories over lunch. But you raise a really interesting question. A company consistently paying a dividend, if purchased at the wrong time — or even more importantly, the wrong price — can be a total disaster. How do you think about valuation and price when you’re making a purchase of a dividend stock?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, it’s interesting. A lot of people have a valuation metric, and valuation is very important to us, both for margin of safety but also just because we think total expected return is relevant to entry price. People with a calculator should be able to verify that I’m right about that. What you pay matters for your total expected return. So the P/E ratio is the most common, and people can use forward or backward. And people look at CAPE, and you can look at price to cash flow, you can look at price to book. I think all these valuation metrics matter. But why is dividend yield itself not a valuation metric — a company’s own historical dividend yield? So there are companies we own right now that have a 2% dividend yield, and they’ve been growing it like crazy, and yet they’ve historically had a three-and-a-half percent dividend yield. It’s just that the stock price is so high.

It pained me, Barry, to sell Walmart about a year and a half ago. I’d owned it my whole career. We made a fortune. Walmart went public the year before I was born and grew the dividend every year of my life. They didn’t do anything wrong. They just happened to go up 60% in one year in stock price. And what had been a three-and-a-half percent dividend yield on average for decades was now one and a half percent — basically an S&P 500-level yield. So from a valuation metric, we sold the stock. Same with Broadcom. The stock was up 16 times. They had grown the dividend 14% per year for eight years in a row. But the yield got to be 1%. So we used the yield as a valuation metric itself.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So we’re recording this the day the book comes out, August 25th, 2026. And this is an era of relatively sticky inflation. We’ve seen 10-year rates and yields come up to almost 5%. We haven’t had a recession in a while, and we certainly haven’t had a major bear market in a while. But I’m curious, how do dividend-yielding stocks and how do dividend growth stocks do in the sort of environment of rising interest rates and high inflation? How do they do during recessions and bear markets?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Well, when you have a beta that is about 0.6 to the market, you naturally have less sensitivity, by definition, to the market itself. The only two stocks in the Dow that were up in 2008 were Walmart and McDonald’s, which were two of the great dividend growers of the last 50 years. They tend to be much more defensive. However, I will also point out that in terms of the offense against inflation, there is no inflation if oil prices aren’t going higher, if cheeseburgers don’t cost more, if soap and towels and Pepsi soda pop don’t cost more. So there’s an inherent inflationary benefit in the fact that the dividend growth has always, in every calendar year, been higher than whatever the growth of prices is — the inflation rate. If you’re getting a portfolio that’s growing dividends from six to 9% and inflation is somewhere between two and 5%, then you are by definition beating inflation in that cash flow. That is, to me, a very important element of the portfolio itself. Whether or not we go into recession, I think that this speaks to the sort of all-weather nature. There’s offense and defense involved in dividend growth.

The last time we had a bad market that was long term — not just the 30 days of COVID or the five days of Liberation Day, but you recall very well both — dot-com lasted two and a half years, from 2000 to 2002; the financial crisis, the market drop was 18 months. And in that period, the S&P was up, from 2000 to 2009, 0%. Most dividend growth portfolios would’ve been up somewhere in the range of seven, 8% per year. So I think that it is a very good time to be looking at it.

Now, what’s a fair question is: hey, but how much did I lose in opportunity cost? The 2009 to 2026 bull market, the S&P’s compounded 15% a year. It doesn’t do me any good to make three or 4% in your stupid dividends while I’m missing that. The fact of the matter is, about half of those years dividend growth has done better than the market. Half of them, not as much. But it’s right there in the same range in a screaming bull market for the index, a screaming low-volatility period where the yield of the S&P is at the lowest it’s ever been.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really, really interesting. One of the criticisms I’ve heard made about dividend growth investing is sometimes investors confuse receiving cash with creating wealth. The classic example is buying a stock right before the dividend issuance, and when it goes ex-dividend, the price falls by the amount of the dividend that gets paid. Tell us what this criticism misses. What’s the mistake there?

DAVID BAHNSEN: Yeah, but when people do that, they fail to understand how markets work. It’s almost like a Treasury Secretary thinking he can buy 30-year bonds and the bond market won’t figure out how these things work.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: I just had that conversation earlier today. I’m like, aren’t you the world’s biggest issuer of debt? How is a tiny announced buyback going to do anything to the long end of that? But go on.

DAVID BAHNSEN: But of course, our Treasury Secretary was himself a global macro trader, and the mentality you bring up about trying to arbitrage dividend payments is something that short-term traders would do as well. So it’s a fine mentality for traders, but it’s a silly mentality in terms of the long-term impact in macroeconomic reality. It doesn’t arbitrage anything to go buy a dividend when markets are pricing in those realities and the algorithmic nature of things can pick up on it ahead of time, et cetera. You are not buying the timing of the receipt of a dividend. You’re buying the company’s underlying growth. You can’t fool the fundamentals.

So I would argue, Barry, that non-dividend investors are doing this far more than dividend investors. Fundamentally, most people that right now believe, “I want to buy the market because there’s someone else who thinks the market’s going to do well. I want to buy Nvidia because there’s someone else who thinks Nvidia’s going to do well” — even if it’s not fully self-conscious, the portfolio strategy of many investors today is dependent on what they think other people will do. Dividend growth investing says I’m isolated to it. I don’t even really need to look at the prices on my screen that much. I believe in the companies executing, growing profits, and growing what they return of that to me over time. And all these other arbitrage things — day by day, week by week, or in some cases nanosecond by nanosecond — are irrelevant to the long-term value creation.

3566f644ebabc6e6: Lifting has been around long before Gen Z. Frances Benjamin Johnston/ Library of Congress/ public domainMore than one quarter of young adults in Britain now say their gym memberships matter more to them than holidays or eating out. Sport England data shows that Gen Z has begun to turn away from running, swimming and fitness classes towards gym and strength training. For them, weight training is seen as the best form of exercise because it can help build strength, improve appearance and boost overall health. People have argued about the best forms of exercise for over two centuries. While today’s fitness trends tend to be more about improving the body and overall fitness, health has rarely been the sole reason why certain exercise trends gained popularity through the eras. Napoleon and gymnastics In 1806, Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Prussia and, inadvertently, created the modern fitness industry. As Napoleon’s troops stormed their way eastward, one Prussian man, Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, began to seethe with anger. For Jahn, Prussian men had lost because they were physically weaker than the French. The nation’s solution, according to Jahn, lay not in muskets – but muscles. So in 1811 Jahn opened a Turnplatz – an open-air gymnasium. Young men ran, jumped, climbed ropes, wrestled and vaulted. They also swung on two pieces of equipment that Jahn is believed to have invented: the parallel bars and the horizontal bar. Soon the trend spread to other nations, with England’s first outdoor gymnastics school opening in 1825. The underlying logic behind Jahn’s Turnplatz system – that strong nations demanded physically strong troops – became a rallying cry for a wave of gymnastic and calisthenic systems for men and women across the century. The birth of bodybuilding A popular form of entertainment in the Victorian era were strongmen shows, where muscular men would perform theatrical acts of strength. One of the most popular performers of the time was Charles “Samson” Sampson, whose act involved snapping chains with his chest. Eugen Sandow became synonymous with the ideal body. The Strobridge Lith. Co., Cin'ti & New York/ Wikimedia Commons But in 1889, a new kind of strongman arrived on the scene. During one of Sampson’s performances, a moustachioed strongman named Eugen Sandow stripped down to his pants in a London theatre, responding to a challenge from Sampson. But what made Sandow different from Sampson and other strongmen of the era was his physique. He was lean and sculpted. From 1889 until his death in 1925, Sandow became synonymous with the ideal body. He was deemed the “best specimen of manhood” by Harvard University physical educationalist Dudley Sargent. Sandow hosted the first major bodybuilding contest in London in 1901 and ran a health enterprise which spread across the British Empire, the Americas and Australasia. Thousands followed his mail-order courses, read his magazine and drank his cocoa. Those lifting dumbbells and barbells to build their bodies like Sandow classed themselves as “physical culturists” in the same way that modern trainees may define themselves by Pilates, Hyrox or weight training. Following Sandow and others, people trained for health but they also trained to become better workers, better spouses, to be more attractive or dynamic. Read more: Fitness gurus and ‘muscular Christianity’: how Victorian Britain anticipated today’s keep fit craze Although the state still mattered – Sandow even trained British troops for the second South African war – the emphasis slowly shifted to building the body for its own sake. The post-war aerobics boom The approach to exercise in the post-war era shifted due to an emerging new health concern: people were sitting down too much. This fear was fuelled by a 1953 work published by epidemiologist Jerry Morris which found that London bus drivers experienced higher instances of heart disease than conductors, who spent their day climbing stairs. The cause? Inactivity. In the US, physicians began rallying against rising heart disease. Their radical solution was to advise people to run slowly for set periods of time – an activity we today call jogging. Pioneered in New Zealand and brought to the US in the 1960s, jogging soon kickstarted an “aerobics” boom. New gym chains filled up with previously untrained enthusiasts running and doing aerobics classes. Aerobics classes were particularly popular with women. And in 1969, fitness instructor Jacki Sorenson originated the aerobics dance movement after she began setting routines to pop music, stitching together steps from jazz, folk, cha-cha and square dancing. Jacki Sorensen pioneered the aerobic dance movement. Employee of Aerobic Dancing, Inc./ Wikimedia Commons The popularity of aerobics only continued to grow throughout the 80s, thanks to actor Jane Fonda’s best-selling 1982 workout video which brought aerobics into the living room. The muscle builders In 1977 the world was introduced to Austrian bodybuilder Arnold Schwarzenegger in the hit documentary Pumping Iron. Brash but charming, muscular but beautiful, Schwarzenegger and the entrepreneur pushing him, Joe Weider, popularised bodybuilding as we now understand it. Pumping Iron hit cinemas at a time when aerobics had driven more people into gyms and new gym equipment made lifting weights far more accessible. Schwarzenegger’s physique soon became a template for heroic figures in pop culture. Action stars, children’s toys and athletes all succumbed to the bodybuilding effect. Leading 80s megastar Sylvester Stallone even transformed his body with Schwarzenegger’s training partner Franco Columbu in preparation for Rambo and the Rocky movies. Women were lifting, too. Lisa Lyon won the first women’s world bodybuilding championship in 1979. Two decades later women’s weightlifting reached the Olympics. By the 2000s, lifting weights was no longer a fringe activity. Budget and 24-hour gyms were commonplace while sports such as CrossFit and powerlifting swelled with men and women. In recent years the hashtag #strongnotskinny has spread across Instagram and TikTok. Exercise scientist Andrew Scott says that influencers have been a big part of this shift. None of this is new. Sandow sold his body on postcards and cocoa tins, Fonda sold hers on VHS and Schwarzenegger sold his at the cinema. Once again, the world around us is changing how people move their bodies. Two hundred years ago, fitness served the country. Now it serves the algorithm. e77076109e4e995b: When telecoms pull out of markets, data protection and human rights commitments often disappear
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Akil Mazumder via Pexels. Used under a Pexels license.
By Jie Zhang

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In March 2022, just over a year after Myanmar’s military coup, Telenor, the Norwegian telecommunications giant, sold its subsidiary in the country to M1 Group, bringing nearly eight years of operation to an end. But leaving Myanmar did not end the controversy surrounding its departure. Instead, the hasty exit came back to haunt the company over the next four years.

Since then, criticisms, lawsuits and litigation by civil society and affected people have continued to follow the company. The scrutiny also reached a crescendo this September, when Norwegian authorities opened criminal investigations into Telenor over allegations of aiding crimes against humanity in the country and transferring sanctioned surveillance equipment during the sale. Within days, a court in Norway also green-lit a class-action lawsuit brought on behalf of a group of Telenor’s former customers in Myanmar.

Telenor reiterated its position upon the investigation, arguing that any alternatives would have endangered the employees’ lives. Yet the company’s trouble raises a broader question that many telecommunication multinationals may have to confront one day: When a company decides to exit a “high-risk market,” where does its responsibility end?
Leaving is not just a business decision

Under military rule, Telenor faced government demands to facilitate surveillance, hand over the personal data of dissidents and activists, and restrict access to information. In a market like this, staying may cease to be viable. For a telecom operator, the matter is not simply to make a choice between remaining in the market or leaving, but whether it can exit in a way that minimizes further harm to users, without leaving them more vulnerable. Unfortunately, Telenor failed to do so.

In a conventional asset sale involving multinational companies, the transaction may center largely around physical and commercial assets, such as factories, equipment, and inventory. Selling a telecom subsidiary is another story. As gatekeepers of internet access and digital information, telcos control sensitive user data, including location records and device logs. They also serve as key intermediaries for interception systems and have the technical capacity to cut off network access. In a sale, the company hands over not just infrastructure and commercial assets, but also systems and data that can expose the movements and footprints of millions of users.

Without rigorous buyer scrutiny and assessments of the risks associated with the transfer, a corporate sale may lead to grave harm to users, who might be watched, tracked, or even silenced in authoritarian contexts.

What followed in Myanmar showed that the risk was anything but hypothetical. It also revealed why powerful companies cannot simply shed their responsibilities by selling their business, when people depending on their services are left to bear the consequences.
A global pull back is underway

This matters because Telenor’s withdrawal from Myanmar is hardly an isolated case. After the debacle, the telecom giant began systematically pulling back from its Asian markets. In 2022, the company combined its Malaysian subsidiary Digi with local telecom service Celcom. In Thailand the following year, it merged its local business dtac with True Corporation before later selling down most of its stake in the entity. It also completed its sale of Telenor Pakistan to PTCL at the end of 2025, with further plans to dispense with its remaining Asian assets.

Zooming out, multinational telecom operators are shrinking the overseas footprints they spent decades building. MTN, Africa’s largest telecom operator, announced its plan to “orderly exit” from the Middle East in 2020 amid geopolitical risks. The company has ended its operations in Syria, Yemen, and Afghanistan by 2025. MTN also completed the sale of its operations in Guinea-Bissau and Guinea-Conakry in 2024, citing unsustainable costs.

Aiming to refocus on a small group of more profitable core markets — Britain, Brazil, Germany, and Spain — Spanish telecom giant Telefónica also accelerated its retreat from Spanish-speaking Latin America. In 2025 alone, it sold its subsidiaries in Argentina, Peru, Uruguay, and Ecuador, followed by exits from Colombia, Chile, and Mexico in early 2026.

The reasons for telecoms’ departure vary from geopolitical tensions to high costs. However, we should ask the critical question: what changes for the customers after a telecom operator leaves them behind?
What gets lost in the handover

While the network will continue to provide service to users, the transparency practices and internal procedures and protocols for data safeguards may change after a sale. This is where the risks of market exit are less visible. Telenor, MTN, and Telefónica have all developed sophisticated governance systems, including formal human rights policies, data-protection and security procedures, and regular transparency reporting. Research shows they are among the strongest performers on transparency and accountability in the telecom industry.

Those transparency reports provide a useful window into how telcos handle government demands. The reports describe the procedures in place to respond to government requests for user data, content restrictions, and network disruptions, and publish data on such requests across different markets. Although transparency alone cannot prevent abuse, it creates a public record of how governments exert pressure on companies.

However, we found that transparency reporting mostly does not survive ownership changes. Once a multinational operator leaves a market, it naturally stops reporting in that country. Disappointingly, its successors overwhelmingly fail to maintain the same level of transparency.

Millicom, a recurring buyer of Telefónica’s Latin American assets, acquired its operations in Uruguay and Ecuador, and a controlling stake in Colombia. Millicom does publish law-enforcement disclosures, but the data are aggregated by region rather than by country. Moreover, as of September 2026, only the 2024 report is publicly available. Elsewhere, the picture is even bleaker: None of the other recent buyers appeared to publish transparency reports or commit to continuing their predecessors’ transparency practices.

The discontinuation of transparency reporting removes the opportunity for the public to scrutinize whether or not the volume of the government demands changed after each ownership transition. It also hides from view how those demands are handled internally.

Transparency reporting, however, is only the tip of the iceberg. Beneath it lies a much broader mechanism of user data protections, institutional norms, and governance safeguards, such as risk escalation channels, legal and human rights checks, and many more.

In authoritarian states, multinational telcos are no less likely to face government pressure to shut down networks, block websites, or hand over user data. While these companies may also have limited room to resist, they usually operate under more institutional oversight than state-controlled ones. They are also exposed to more scrutiny from the international press and civil society, greater reputational risk, and often stronger regulatory frameworks established by their home countries.

By contrast, many operators who succeeded these businesses might be more closely connected to governments and more deeply embedded in the local political and regulatory environment. Facing fewer external constraints from society, media, and NGOs, they also have less willingness and fewer resources to challenge governments.
What a more responsible exit might look like

Since safeguards may weaken or even disappear with ownership shift, the essential duty to protect users’ rights should not be treated as an afterthought to a market exit. It must be a key element of the transaction.

For telecom companies, a responsible exit should begin well before a buyer is even selected. Before entering Myanmar in 2014, Telenor commissioned a human rights impact assessment (HRIA) for its planned market entry. The company also states that it considered human rights and data privacy as it prepared for its departure. But there is no public record showing that Telenor conducted a standalone assessment of the human rights risks of the exit itself.

Companies should commission a mandated, exit-specific human rights impact assessment, evaluating what user risks the sale itself might create, the concerns of stakeholders and users, how the data might be used or transferred in the future, and which groups of users would be most exposed to the risks it identifies.

Buyer due diligence should go beyond financial stability to examine the buyer’s human rights record, its capacity to govern sensitive data, and whether existing safeguards can survive under new ownership.

Moreover, a responsible exit from any politically risky market should also ask a basic question: What should not be transferred in a sale? Should every piece of user data be handed over to the next owner? Telecom companies should evaluate if any sensitive data can be segregated, anonymized, or even deleted whenever feasible, particularly when transferring such data could expose high-risk users.

Similarly, some technical infrastructure, such as surveillance equipment, interception systems, and other network-control capabilities, should not be bundled into a sale automatically as ordinary infrastructure. Norwegian authorities are now probing whether Telenor transferred sanctioned surveillance equipment as part of the sale of Telenor Myanmar without the required authorization from the Norwegian government.
A new test for the next exit

If Telenor offers a lesson for everyone about what can go wrong in a reckless departure from a high-risk market, MTN’s unfinished exit from Iran may offer a test about whether companies can approach their next departure differently.

MTN still holds a 49 percent stake in Irancell. The current U.S. sanctions on Iran also complicate any attempt to exit. Earlier this year, MTN also protested after the CEO of Irancell was ousted by the Iranian authorities over delaying an internet blackout order during the domestic protest. This arguably makes MTN’s position in Iran even more difficult than Telenor’s trajectory in Myanmar. When MTN is finally able to withdraw from the country, can it exit in a more responsible way?

eb3a7b0a074d9b95: Russia has traded highly trained operatives for cheap technology and expendable recruits. DC Studio / ShutterstockRussian hostile activity costs the UK at least £2 billion annually, according to a recent report by Scottish MP Graeme Downie, who has called on the government to measure what these actions cost Britain. But this figure is just the baseline. In reality, a profound shift in Moscow’s approach to sabotage means the true cost is set to climb higher. While Russia still draws on its cold war target lists, ranging from critical transit nodes and military sites; to energy and communication infrastructure; it has traded highly trained operatives for cheap technology and expendable recruits. The switch to a quantity-over-quality model presents a much more volatile threat. This model borrows from the logic of distributed computing. It uses networks of cheap, unreliable parts where individual breakdowns are expected yet the overall system still gets the job done. By generating a high volume of low-cost operations that often fail at the individual level, Moscow still achieves its objectives of causing outsized psychological disruption and steadily exhausting western security services. A 2024 arson attack on a London warehouse is one of a number of sabotage attempts European authorities believe Russia has ordered in recent years. This operational transformation surged after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Within months, over 400 Russian intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover were expelled across Europe. This number has since climbed to more than 700. The mass purge was expected to cripple Russia’s spy networks. But it instead accelerated Moscow’s pivot towards what research I carried out with colleagues in 2024 defined as “gig-economy” operatives. In place of declared “diplomats” well known to local counterintelligence officers, operations have been outsourced to disposable proxies recruited for a pittance. These people are often unaware of who their handlers are or their mission’s real goals. This new campaign brings to life former CIA chief James Woolsey’s 1993 description of the post-cold war security landscape as a “jungle of venomous snakes”. Gig-economy operatives Recruited on messaging apps and paid in cryptocurrency, gig-economy operatives have been tasked with arson and other property damage, beatings, kidnappings and assassinations. This includes assassination plots on US soil in a stark breach of cold war conventions. While many of these plots have been amateurish, the intent behind them and their potential damage is real. Blurring the lines between theatrics and physical damage, the campaigns have included mock coffins placed beneath the Eiffel Tower and graffiti designed to stoke antisemitic tensions across Paris. Arson targets have ranged from a warehouse in London storing aid for Ukraine to an Ikea store in Lithuania and a paint factory in Poland. Western intelligence also narrowly averted catastrophe in 2025 when incendiary devices planted on DHL cargo planes caught fire in freight depots on the ground rather than mid-flight. Beyond commercial property, Moscow’s campaign has targeted critical infrastructure. At sea, the playbook has escalated from plausible deniability to overt military posturing. Since 2023, Russian-linked commercial vessels flagged from China to the Cook Islands have repeatedly severed power and data cables by dragging their anchors across the seabed. The Russian authorities have backed this with hard power. This has ranged from scrambling fighter jets to deter Estonian authorities from approaching a suspected vessel in 2025, to deploying intelligence ships and submarines close to western lines. A parallel escalation has unfolded in the air. Operations began with electronic interference and drone surveillance disrupting commercial aviation, as well as probing European military bases and transport hubs to test air defences and map blind spots and vulnerabilities. They have since graduated to overt airspace violations by Russian military aircraft and missiles, while armed drones have repeatedly crashed or detonated in Polish, Latvian and Moldovan territory. This pattern crossed from deniable sabotage into a direct physical attack in August 2026 when an explosives-laden drone crashed into the wing of a parked Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany. The device failed to detonate, averting a major explosion on an aircraft that had previously transported military ammunition. The incident exposed not only Moscow’s escalatory ambitions, but also the sharp decline in professionalism within Russian intelligence. Rather than the elite officers cold war doctrine called for, the Russian intelligence handler relied on amateur recruits, who botched the job. Yet for Moscow, operational failures are almost as useful as successes. A botched strike still generates media panic, exhausts European security services and projects a menacing shadow far beyond Russia’s real capabilities. Moscow’s cyber campaigns The same logic underpins the Kremlin’s cyber campaigns, where merely threatening critical infrastructure is often enough to achieve intimidation. Cyberattacks on a Norwegian dam and a Swedish heating plant, both in 2025, caused negligible physical damage. But they generated alarming headlines and have had psychological effects. Also in 2025, a cyberattack on a major Polish power and heating plant threatened to cut heat to half a million people during winter. Even though blackouts were avoided, the destructive potential was impossible to ignore. In cyber operations, as in physical sabotage, the perpetrators range from opportunistic proxies like the pro-Russian hackers in Sweden to elite hacking units directed by Russian intelligence in Poland. Across domains, Russia has turned unpredictability and disruption into its strategic weapon of choice. Using expendable, poorly trained proxies directed remotely by state handlers consistently achieves psychological disruption while narrowly averting casualties through operational failure. However, relying on Russian incompetence to protect European lives cannot hold. As the old maxim goes: hope is not a strategy.
